title: Astronomers Discover a Possible New Dwarf Planet in Our Solar System
gist: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found 2026 ED138, a trans-Neptunian object 600-1,500 km across at about 46 AU that could become the sixth IAU-recognized dwarf planet, hidden until now against the Milky Way's disk. Its trajectory was reconstructed from archival images back to 2016.

insights.claim: Astronomers at the Vera C. Rubin Observatory found 2026 ED138, a trans-Neptunian object measuring 600 to 1,500 kilometers across at about 46 astronomical units from the sun, possibly one of the brightest and largest of its type.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Rubin's survey output is starting to yield headline discoveries in the outer solar system.

insights.claim: Matthew Holman identified the object on October 13 and the team found archival observations back to 2016, reconstructing more than a decade of its trajectory.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Archival data mining multiplies the value of new survey detections.

insights.claim: ED138 had stayed hidden because it lies against the disk of the Milky Way, where star density masks faint objects, and Rubin's enormous data volume made identification possible.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Big-data astronomy can resolve objects in previously unsearchable regions of the sky.

insights.claim: ED138 would join Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris as the sixth IAU-recognized dwarf planet if its size proves sufficient for gravity to make it nearly spherical.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: Confirmation hinges on precise size measurement, which distance makes difficult.
insights.locator: Though ED138 appears to have the right characteristics

insights.claim: Dozens of outer-solar-system objects, including Gonggong, Quaoar, Sedna and Orcus, are candidates for dwarf-planet status but are hard to confirm because distance prevents direct measurement of size and mass.
insights.speaker: Jorge Garay
insights.so_what: The catalog of solar system bodies is likely to grow as survey capacity rises.
